title: Detect Subversion of Trust Controls via Certificate, Registry, and Attribute Manipulation
shortTitle: Detect Subversion of Trust Controls via Certificate, Regi...
summary: This strategy detects subversion of trust controls, meaning changes to the certificates, registry entries, or file attributes that Windows and other platforms use to decide whether code and connections are trustworthy. It matters because weakening one trust decision lets an attacker run unsigned code, intercept traffic, or bypass the checks that would otherwise stop them, and the change is usually small. Detection relies on registry modification telemetry for the certificate and trust store keys, file creation records inside the trusted root and publisher stores, and certificate installation events, joined with process creation to identify the tool that made the change. It fails when certificate services are managed by automation that edits the stores constantly, because the same write that is routine on a build server is suspicious on a user laptop.

beginner.definition: Computers keep lists of certificates, which are digital identity documents, and registry settings that say which software is trusted. This detection watches for changes to those lists and settings. An attacker who changes them can make harmful software look approved.
beginner.whyItMatters: Trust settings decide what your computer will run and which secure connections it accepts. If an attacker weakens a trust setting, later checks pass when they should fail. The edit itself is often tiny, so it is easy to miss among normal activity.
howItWorks: A sensor records every change to registry keys that hold trust and certificate settings.
The rule compares the changed key or file path with a list of trust related locations.
It records which process performed the write and which account it used.
It also collects certificate installation events and their thumbprints.
The analyst checks whether the certificate or setting is known and approved.
An unapproved certificate added by a script host raises an alert for review.
beginner.example: Think of a building where the front desk keeps a book of approved delivery companies. Someone adds a new company to the book in pencil. The guards then wave through any van with that name, even a van nobody ordered.
takeaways: Trust stores and trust registry keys decide what the system believes.
Small edits to those places can unlock much larger actions later.
Always check which process made the change and when it ran.

objectives: Explain what a certificate store and trust registry key control
Identify telemetry that records trust store writes and certificate installs
Recognise the difference between a managed rollout and a local trust edit
Correlate a trust change with the tool and user that performed it
Escalate a review when an unknown certificate appears in a root store
dataSources: Sysmon event 13 registry value set for certificate and trust related keys under the system certificate stores
Sysmon event 11 file creation records inside the trusted root and trusted publisher certificate store directories
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled
Windows certificate services client lifecycle events that record installed and removed certificates
Linux auditd file watches on the system certificate bundle and update trust store directories
logic: The pattern is a write to a location that defines trust, made by a process that does not normally manage trust. Correlate the registry key or file path, the value written, the process image and its signature state, the parent process, and the user account, then match the certificate thumbprint against your approved inventory. The benign case is an enterprise certificate authority rollout driven by group policy or a mobile device management agent, where the parent process is the management service, the certificate matches a published thumbprint, and the write happens inside a change window. The malicious case is a local write to a trust store by an interactive shell or an unsigned tool, a certificate that is not in the inventory, or a value that disables a trust check, such as a registry setting that switches off signature or revocation checking.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Certificate store or trust registry key modified by unmanaged tool
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 13
#     TargetObject|contains:
#       - '\\Microsoft\\SystemCertificates\\Root\\Certificates'
#       - '\\Microsoft\\SystemCertificates\\TrustedPublisher\\Certificates'
#       - '\\Cryptography\\Configuration\\OID\\'
#   filter_managed:
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\\ccmexec.exe'
#       - '\\certutil.exe'
#       - '\\mdmagent.exe'
#   condition: selection and not filter_managed
# level: high
falsePositives: Enterprise certificate authorities that push new root certificates through group policy or mobile device management
Internal development teams installing a self signed certificate for a test service on a lab machine
Backup or configuration management tooling that writes the certificate store as part of image deployment
Security products that add or refresh their own inspection certificate during an agent upgrade
tuningNotes: Filter by the signing state and parent process of the writing tool rather than by the tool name alone, because certificate utilities are also abused. Keep an inventory of approved certificate thumbprints and alert on anything new, especially in a root store. Scope the rule to user workstations and internet facing servers first, and exclude the build and certificate authority hosts where these writes are constant. If you filter certutil entirely you lose the very tool most often used for the download and install step, so keep a separate rule that alerts on certutil install actions that are not tied to a change record.
